issues.legal_issue: The bar against a separate suit to set aside a compromise decree does not prevent a court from examining the decree in a challenge by an aggrieved devotee where fraud or collusion by officers of a statutory authority is made out.
material_facts: A devotee who was not a party to the civil suit challenged the compromise in a writ proceeding.

The compromise involved a statutory board and was alleged to have been collusive; the circumstances showed that the board had agreed to give up temple property in exchange for property already in the temple’s possession.
The board had previously been directed by court orders to take possession of the property it agreed to give up.
issues.conclusion: The bar in Order 23 Rule 3A of the Code of Civil Procedure did not prevent examination of the compromise decree, and the devotee’s challenge could not be rejected merely because the devotee was not a party to the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Order 23 Rules 3 and 3A of the Code of Civil Procedure regulate compromise decrees and bar a separate suit to set aside a decree on the ground that its compromise was unlawful. That bar does not prevent the High Court from examining a compromise decree when fraud or collusion by officers of a statutory authority is made out, including on a challenge by an aggrieved devotee who was not a party to the suit. The Court also relied on the earlier orders directing the board to take possession of the property.

rule.if: devotee_challenges_compromise_in_writ and challenger_not_party_to_suit and compromise_decree_exists and statutory_authority_party and officers_fraud_or_collusion_made_out

predicates.devotee_challenges_compromise_in_writ: A devotee brings a writ challenge to a compromise decree.
predicates.challenger_not_party_to_suit: The devotee bringing the challenge was not a party to the suit in which the compromise decree was made.
predicates.compromise_decree_exists: A civil court has entered a decree in terms of a compromise.
predicates.statutory_authority_party: A statutory authority was a party to the compromise.
predicates.officers_fraud_or_collusion_made_out: Fraud or collusion by officers of the statutory authority in entering the compromise is made out.

issues.definition: When a non-party devotee challenges a compromise decree in a writ proceeding and fraud or collusion by officers of a statutory authority is made out, the challenge is not barred merely because it concerns a compromise decree.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory board cannot validly compromise away religious-institution property contrary to a direction to take possession when the exchange gives the institution property it already possesses and the court that issued the direction has not permitted the compromise.
material_facts: The board had been directed to take possession of land belonging to a temple.
The board agreed to transfer that land to claimants in exchange for other land that was already in the temple’s possession and contained structures housing deities.
The board’s own resolution recorded that the exchange land was already in the temple’s possession.
The board entered the compromise without obtaining permission from the court that had directed it to take possession of the land.
The compromise decree was challenged on appeal after the High Court dismissed a devotee’s writ petition.
issues.conclusion: The compromise and compromise decree could not be sustained; they were set aside, and the board was directed to take possession of the land as previously ordered.
issues.legal_principle: Property of deities, temples, and religious institutions must be protected and safeguarded by those entrusted with its management, and courts must protect it from wrongful claims or misappropriation. A board’s settlement giving away temple property in exchange for property already in the temple’s possession is improper where the board had been directed to take possession and did not obtain permission from the court that issued that direction. The Court relied on the prior High Court and Supreme Court orders concerning possession, as well as Order 23 Rules 3 and 3A of the Code of Civil Procedure in addressing the compromise decree.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_dismissal_of_devotee_writ and board_compromised_temple_property and prior_court_order_required_possession and exchange_property_already_in_temple_possession and court_permission_not_obtained

predicates.appeal_challenges_dismissal_of_devotee_w: An appeal challenges the dismissal of a devotee’s writ proceeding against a compromise decree.
predicates.board_compromised_temple_property: A board responsible for religious-institution property agreed to transfer property belonging to that institution under a compromise.
predicates.prior_court_order_required_possession: A prior court order directed the board to take possession of the property it agreed to transfer.
predicates.exchange_property_already_in_temple_poss: The property offered in exchange was already in the religious institution’s possession.
predicates.court_permission_not_obtained: The board entered the compromise without permission from the court that had directed it to take possession.

issues.definition: When a board compromises away religious-institution property despite a prior possession direction, receives property already held by the institution in exchange, and lacks permission from the court that issued the direction, the compromise decree is set aside and possession is required.

issues.legal_issue: An official inquiry and remedial action are warranted where an order assigning religious-institution land arose in suspicious circumstances involving an institutional employee.
material_facts: A person employed by the temple was shown as a cultivating tenant of land in front of the temple containing structures housing deities.
The assignment order was made in suo motu proceedings and was ex parte.

The circumstances raised a concern that the order might have been obtained through collusion with revenue officials; it was also pointed out that the order did not refer to the relevant survey number.
issues.conclusion: The Collector was directed to inquire into the circumstances in which the assignment order was made and to take consequential remedial action.
issues.legal_principle: The property of religious institutions must be protected from wrongful claims and misappropriation. Where the circumstances surrounding an order affecting such property raise concerns of collusion or improper acquisition, the Court may direct an official inquiry and consequential remedial action. No earlier case was cited for this direction.

predicates.appeal_concerns_religious_institution_pr: An appeal concerns property belonging to a religious institution.
predicates.land_assignment_order_exists: An order assigned or purported to assign land associated with the religious institution.
predicates.institutional_employee_claimed_tenancy: An employee of the institution was treated as a tenant or cultivating tenant of the land.
predicates.assignment_proceeding_was_ex_parte_or_su: The assignment proceeding was ex parte or its circumstances otherwise raised a concern of improper or collusive acquisition.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerning religious-institution property reveals an assignment order involving an institutional employee and suspicious or ex parte proceedings, an official inquiry and remedial action are ordered.
